title: 105 Elmira Road apartment proposal and 72 Gordon Street heritage tie
subtitle: Heritage designation vote deadlocked and deferred to June; sign by-law amendments received for feedback; traffic, parking and unit mix concerns.
overview: Council held a statutory public meeting on a proposed six-storey, 126-unit rental apartment building at 105 Elmira Road North. The applicant wants to change the land use from neighbourhood commercial to medium density residential, with several site-specific zoning exceptions. Council received the application {{vote:m1}}. No decision was made; staff will bring a recommendation report to a later public meeting. Councillors asked about the Willow Road access, parking, density, the lack of three-bedroom units and the absence of commercial space.

On 72 Gordon Street, the owner objected to a notice of intention to designate the building under the Ontario Heritage Act. Council received the objection {{vote:m3}}, but a motion to approve the designation by-law was defeated {{vote:m4}}. A motion to withdraw the notice also failed {{vote:m5}}. Council then deferred the matter to the June 10, 2025 planning meeting {{vote:m6}}. Staff said the notice lapses if no designation motion is brought forward by July 25.

Council also received a staff report on proposed Sign By-law amendments {{vote:m7}}. These mainly update zone names to match the 2023 zoning by-law and add a few new rules. No decision was needed. Council approved five by-laws {{vote:m8}}.

decisions.detail: Council received the application for an Official Plan and Zoning By-law Amendment for the proposed apartment building, with no decision on the merits yet.
Council received the property owner's notice of objection to the intention to designate 72 Gordon Street {{vote:m3}}.
A motion to approve the heritage designation by-law was defeated on a tie {{vote:m4}}, so the designation was not approved.
A motion to withdraw the notice of intention to designate under the Ontario Heritage Act also failed on a tie {{vote:m5}}.
Council deferred the objection and designation question to the June 10, 2025 Council Planning meeting {{vote:m6}}.
Council received the City-initiated report on amendments to the Sign By-law (2021)-20621, which staff will revise after feedback {{vote:m7}}.

debate: Councillors questioned the requested exceptions: 130 units per hectare against a 100 maximum, fewer parking spaces, less amenity space and all-surface parking. The applicant's planner said the extra units would add rental supply and cited cost as the reason for no underground parking. A councillor noted the site is flat and undeveloped and asked why the standard zoning could not be met.

Neighbouring residents and delegates raised traffic and safety concerns. They pointed to the Willow Road entrance near the school, cut-through traffic on a nearby street, overflow parking, and privacy and lighting from the parking lot. One delegate asked that the entrance be moved to Elmira Road. The applicant said Elmira did not meet the 100-metre distance from the intersection, and staff will confirm the figure.

Several councillors and delegates asked for family-sized three-bedroom units, since the plan has only one- and two-bedroom units. Some also asked for ground-floor commercial space. The applicant said commercial was considered and found not viable, and that a study found enough commercial space nearby.

Affordability was questioned. The applicant said the federal financing program requires at least 20% of units to rent below a set income-based threshold. A delegate doubted that new construction could be affordable.

On 72 Gordon Street, one councillor argued the designation would burden the owner and limit redevelopment. The heritage planner said only the Gordon and Surrey street walls would be protected and that designation allows flexibility, including relocating or rebuilding those walls. Other councillors stressed protecting the last remnant of the area's history, and staff said no heritage grants are currently available.

On the sign by-law, councillors asked about a shut-off time for illuminated rear signs facing homes, brightness limits, dark-sky rules, and signs in heritage areas. Staff said the scope is limited and will take these questions back.
